title: James Gunn Releases Statement Following Departure As DC Studios Co-Head
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Robert Pattinson & Nicholas Hoult Round Out James Bond Screen Tests Teyonah Parris To Co-Star With Denzel Washington In Christopher McQuarrie’s Thriller For United Artists Nicholas Galitzine Eyeing Ichabod Crane Role In Sony’s ‘Hollow’ Starring Sydney Sweeney View All November 9, 2026 11:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source James Gunn Theo Wargo / Getty Images Following the news that he and Peter Safran would no longer be co-running DC Studios following the Skydance-Warner Bros. merger, James Gunn has spoken out about his time running the studio. The lengthy statement which Gunn dropped on his social media platforms goes into detail how proud his four years were touching on all the projects made while also touching on his partnership with Safran, who he described as “the smartest most competent person” he’s know. Gunn also touched ono how trying the four years had been and how he had grown to “dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job.” The statement comes after Skydance chose to replace Gunn and Safran with veteran exec Latcham as the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. Gunn and Safran will continue to produce on various DC projects and returning to their full-time creative work. They’re currently in post on the Superman sequel, Man of Tomorrow which will open in theaters on July 9, 2027. Related Stories News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In News John Constantine Movie From 'Evil Dead Wrath's Francis Galluppi In Development At DC Gunn released the statement on his social media platforms and you can read it in full below: Watch on Deadline “Oh, boy. What a four years.” “Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios. When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.” “There have been so many highs along the way – releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs, the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments.” “The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran, the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.” “But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head.” So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on. Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen. Love and gratitude, James Gunn View this post on Instagram ‘Yellowstone’s Cole Hauser Preps FBI Action Thriller ‘Pale Horse’ With Eye To Star ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $32M U.S. Bow, Best For Live-Action Foreign-Language Pic 10½-Year Prison Sentence; Survivor Speaks Out, Rips Channel 4 De Niro Targets Elon At ‘Musk’ Documentary Screening On GOP Spending Spree Read More About: Comments

title: Alex Proyas Takes Over Directing Duties On AI-Enabled Historical Drama ‘Cortés’ Starring Antonio Banderas; Filming Underway — AFM
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Andreas Wiseman Andreas Wiseman Executive Editor, Film & International @AndreasWiseman More Stories By Andreas The Hunt For The Next ‘Obsession’ Continues At AFM, Where A24’s ‘Elden Ring’ & New Films With Jeremy Renner, Idris Elba, Gillian Anderson & Renée Zellweger Hit The Market: Hot List + Analysis Jonathan Bailey & Bill Nighy To Star In Love Story ‘Insomniac City’ For Director Dominic Cooke — AFM Al Munteanu’s German Outfit BriskPace Confirms Leadership Team View All November 9, 2026 11:32am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Alex Proyas and Antonio Banderas Courtesy/Jesus Chacon EXCLUSIVE : I, Robot and Dark City filmmaker Alex Proyas is taking over directing duties on Cortés , the historical epic starring Oscar nominee Antonio Banderas as Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés. Filming began in Paris and Spain a few weeks ago with French filmmaker Paul Mignot announced at the time as helming the project. Proyas has subsequently taken over. According to the production, “Mignot remains attached to the project in another capacity.” No reason was given for his directing exit. The AI-enabled film, written by Oscar nominee Nicholas Kazan ( Reversal of Fortune ) and produced by Marco Weber is co-financed and co-produced by Utopai Studios and Ex Machina Studios. Related Stories News The Hunt For The Next 'Obsession' Continues At AFM, Where A24's 'Elden Ring' & New Films With Jeremy Renner, Idris Elba, Gillian Anderson & Renée Zellweger Hit The Market: Hot List + Analysis Casting Adam Devine & Chloe Fineman Set For Michael Diliberti Crime Comedy 'Miami PI' - AFM It marks Proyas’ highest-profile movie since he made big-budget Lionsgate action pic Gods Of Egypt a decade ago. The announcement comes as the companies head into the American Film Market ( AFM ), where sales partner K5 International, under the Ex Machina sales label, will be looking to sell the project to buyers in Europe, Latin America, Australia and New Zealand. Utopai Studios controls distribution rights throughout the rest of the world, including North America and Asia. Set in 1519, “ Cortés begins in Cuba, where a restless soldier hungry for glory seizes command of an expedition to the Yucatán and sails without permission. After landing on the coast of what is now Mexico, he meets Marina, an enslaved Indigenous woman and gifted linguist who becomes indispensable to his advance. As Cortés turns fragile alliances, faith and fear into instruments of conquest, Marina watches him transform from a daring outlaw into a self-anointed messiah.” Proyas said today: “ Cortés is one of cinema’s great untold stories — a tale of ambition, conquest and betrayal, told through the eyes of the extraordinary woman who helped shape the course of history. Nicholas has written a script of remarkable scale and intimacy, exploring a man of profound contradictions — visionary and ruthless, charismatic and monstrous, capable of extraordinary courage and unspeakable cruelty. With Antonio, we have an actor who can inhabit every facet of that complexity. My collaboration with Marco and the Ex Machina team on Heaven has opened up exhilarating new possibilities for cinematic storytelling, allowing us to bring this extraordinary world to life on a scale and with a visual ambition that would once have been unimaginable.” The filmmaker, also known for movies The Crow and Knowing , most recently produced the 2023 thriller Mercy Road starring Luke Bracey and Toby Jones and is is on production on Ex Machina project Heaven , which is due for release in 2027. He’s also been in post on comedy musical R.U.R. in recent years. Watch on Deadline Mignot’s previous credits include the historical feature Vaincre ou Mourir . He has also directed campaigns for BMW, Porsche, Audi, Lexus, Jeep, L’Oréal, Louis Vuitton, and Emporio Armani. ‘Yellowstone’s Cole Hauser Preps FBI Action Thriller ‘Pale Horse’ With Eye To Star ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $32M U.S. Bow, Best For Live-Action Foreign-Language Pic 10½-Year Prison Sentence; Survivor Speaks Out, Rips Channel 4 De Niro Targets Elon At ‘Musk’ Documentary Screening On GOP Spending Spree Read More About: Comments

title: Son Lux Says Its ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Score Reflected The Islamic Faith – Sound & Screen Film
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Fred Topel Fred Topel More Stories By Fred ‘Project Hail Mary’ Composer Daniel Pemberton Built “A Language From The Ground Up” Using New Instruments – Sound & Screen Film ‘Alien: Earth’ Composer Jeff Russo Used An Aztec Death Whistle For His Xenomorph Theme – Sound & Screen TV ‘All Her Fault’ Composer Jeff Beal Used Music To Give Mystery Series’ Duplicitous Characters The Benefit Of The Doubt – Sound & Screen TV View All November 9, 2026 11:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source There are not many Muslim action movies, so Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is already unique. Its music reflects the disparate elements at play in the film, too. Son Lux wrote the score for the Orion Pictures / Amazon MGM Studios film, as well the song “Now I’m Listening,” which singer-songwriter Bilal performs with them. The band members Rafiq Bhatia, Ian Chang and Ryan Lott spoke about reflecting the movie’s themes in the music in a virtual Q&A for Sound & Screen Film. Your Mother stars Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devout Muslim hit man. Bassam Tariq wrote and directed; many of Son Lux’s inspirations came from Tariq, they band said. Related Stories News Deadline Launches Its Contenders London Streaming Site Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Tonys, Guilds & More “A big part of the Islamic faith is that there’s this unknowable, ineffable feeling,” Chang said. “That was something that was very important to Bassam, he told us from the beginning, this kind of almost mystery with something that needed to be communicated in a way that was both dealing with mystery and the majesty of the unknowable.” Tariq also encouraged Son Lux to utilize a vocal choir in the music. Lott said it led the band “to really investigate the power of the human voice both individually and also collectively. We found the soul of the score upon his urging to investigate more aggressively the use of the human voice.” A choir sings “Now I’m Listening” at Sound & Screen Film JC Olivera for Deadline The human choir more specifically incorporates Sufi Zikr chants. Bhatia said Son Lux drew from real men facing violence. “Some of the most unforgettable ones were these Chechen rebels that were preparing for battle and doing chanting Zikr and doing breath work,” Bhatia said. With vocalization, Son Lux could repeat words and phrases. This also reflected Islamic philosophies. “In Islamic artwork and architecture, there is this idea of infinite geometry of these patterns that repeat endlessly to give an expression to the otherwise inexpressible, to communicate infinity,” Bhatia said. “Even if you truncate the Islamic creed and you just say ‘La ilaha,’ ‘There is no god.’ Or ‘La ilaha il,’ ‘There is no god but,’ if you take that and repeat it as an infinite pattern, that expression of doubt made infinite is actually its own expression of the infinite and the unknowable.” Lott also credits Bilal with bringing their song to life. title: ‘The Gilded Age’ Is Serving Up Ambition and Shame in Season 4 Return
full_text: Skip to main content By Ronda Racha Penrice Plus Icon Ronda Racha Penrice View All November 9, 2026 11:12am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Morgan Spector and Carrie Coon in 'The Gilded Age' season four. HBO Logo text [This story contains spoilers from The Gilded Age season four premiere.] The Gilded Age is officially back. And while that world is still turning, it’s not quite moving in the way many fans had predicted. After a third season filled with dramatic deaths and near-deaths — not to mention an arranged marriage motivated by power and position later punished with an unexpected sacrifice of the heart and an exciting wedding proposal — season four’s first episode “Ring the Bells,” directed by executive producer Salli Richardson-Whitfield , immediately kicks off with another seesaw of emotions. Related Stories TV Chuck Lorre Talks David Ellison Optimism, Scientology and the Perks (Really!) of Working for Roseanne Barr Movies 'All That She Wants' Review: Annie Murphy Is All That in a Fizzy Rom-Com That Works Best When It Isn't Trying Too Hard In England, Gladys — as many women, even the wealthy ones, of that era did — experiences the life-threatening birth of her first child with the loving Duke she was forced to marry, and now adores, by her side , while Oscar van Rhijn trades “I do’s” with his bride ( yes, bride! ) Enid Winterton, the new Mrs. Oscar van Rhijn. Gilded Age creator, executive producer and writer Julian Fellowes tells The Hollywood Reporter that the first episode featured the van Rhijn wedding because “we wanted to have the fun of catching everyone out so that at the beginning they think that they’re going to be watching one of the weddings they’ve been expecting, and this is one of them they haven’t been expecting.” Element of surprise aside, Fellowes adds that “it’s nice to have a group scene to start a series off. You want to show a lot of your characters and the world they’re operating in so that your public can become reacquainted with the whole setup. If you start a series with a two-hander of two people sitting in a sitting room talking, it doesn’t quite do the same thing. You’re saying to the viewer, ‘You’re back in our world, and here we all are.’” This season, the show feels even more personal. “We wanted to test all of the relationships within the show. So marriages, romances, familial relationships. I think the social mobility that is inherent to America is also something that’s tested, and we get to see who gets to move up socially, where they get to go,” says Fellowes’ The Gilded Age collaborator Sonja Warfield, who serves as executive producer and writer alongside Fellowes. Newly rich Jack, who still feels a servant at heart, demonstrates some of those social growing pains. “When he enters into society with all of these, to him, sort of fruitless and sometimes aimless rules around how to behave and how to operate with power, he’s having to decide for himself how much he wants to play in that space, especially with how much he’s already sacrificed to be here,” Ben Ahlers explained during The Gilded Age press conference at New York City’s iconic The Plaza Hotel. “The negotiation that I think all of these characters really, in the end, have to make, is: what are they willing to sacrifice for what they feel is right for them?” he added. George Russell, with his self-imposed estrangement from Bertha, a storyline that carries directly over from last season’s finale , seems to be renegotiating his position to both wealth and family when most feel, like Carrie Coon who embodies Bertha, that “George needs to get his act together.” “We’d set up in the previous season that this extremely well-balanced and well-suited marriage was beginning to hit a rather rocky period, which I think is no more than real life. In films, everyone’s happy ever after — but nobody’s happy ever after in life. We wanted to go on with that and explore it, and see the extent to which they could come together again or not,” says Fellowes. The first episode hints that George is clearly not himself. With another business crisis on hand, he’s even barking at their son Larry (Harry Richardson). Investigators may have also found George’s would-be assassin. “It’s a total life reset for George,” is how Morgan Spector explained his character dynamic during the press conference at The Plaza Hotel. “His relationship with Bertha, has, if not collapsed, at least fallen on hard times. He’s been nearly killed and he also failed his daughter [Gladys] catastrophically. “For George,” he continued, “the relationships with Gladys and Bertha — not so much with Larry — are central to his concept of himself as a good human being. He’s really failed in both of these areas, and his capacity to compartmentalize and be business-ruthless, but loving father at home, is all out the window. Now he’s got to figure out how he can think of himself as a decent person and what his principles really are going forward. That’s all at play in this season.” After nearly losing Gladys ( Taissa Farmiga ), and sparring with Lady Sarah (Hattie Morahan), the duke’s sister, over why a mother would choose her child over the male heir if only one could be saved during childbirth, Bertha is at least pleased that Hector (Ben Lamb), the duke, if it came down to it, chose to save his wife over his child, his heir. “Gladys is doing great, and Bertha feels vindicated about that,” he says. Had Gladys been able to choose between herself and the baby, Farmiga, who is not a mother herself, tells THR , that since “there’s such a high mortality rate for infants at that time, it’s expected that something is probably going to go wrong. And I think at that point she would probably choose herself for the first one, at least.” While Bertha has secured Gladys’ future and place in society, Enid, her former lady’s maid who made a play for George, is still on a journey to lock hers down. “Social mobility and so on and so forth are all represented in the wedding of Oscar and Enid where they are marrying for many reasons, but none of them have to do with romantic love. And you know that was a reminder that we’re back in this very worldly group,” says Fellowes. “She just wants power,” Kelly Curran said of Enid. “And society is her runway to achieve that. Just as Oscar doesn’t have to hide his homosexuality from her, she doesn’t have to hide her ambition. “She sort of ascends each season,” Curran explained. “Now, she has the full support of the van Rhijn family name and this partner who’s really her best friend. It’s an incredible trajectory. So not only can she feel that kind of security and support for the first time in her life, but now she can do something with it. She has a vision and she has taste and she plans.” “They are very unified in their vision of a new society,” Blake Ritson chimed in of Enid and Oscar’s pairing. “Even though they come from very different backgrounds, they’re kind of kindred spirits. They like being disruptors, effectively.” Their union also brings hope to Oscar’s mother Agnes van Rhijn, played by the fantastic Christine Baranski . Fresh off the wedding, she’s downright giddy about hosting a dinner for Grover Cleveland, the President of the United States, as vice-president of the New York Historical Society in the home she shares with her sister Ada Forte. After grieving her husband’s death last season, Ada is finding a new sense of confidence which includes saying no to funding Agnes’s presidential dinner. That leaves an opening for Enid. While news of her daughter-in-law’s servant past doesn’t thrill Agnes, Enid’s ability to finance her dinner does. Cynthia Nixon , who plays Ada, loves Agnes’s new attitude. “One of the delightful and hilarious things that we get to see this season is unhinged Agnes,” she shared. “The ambitions of the Gilded Age were worldly ones,” Fellowes reminds us. “This was not a particularly spiritual society. And they weren’t wrestling as we are where everyone’s always trying to look nowadays like the most generous, charitable person on earth. And you ask any film star what they care about and they go ‘well, what I care about is the destruction of the environment.’ Really, what they care about is what their agent has managed to get with the size of their trailer, but they don’t want to say that, and so they create this illusion. “Well, similarly, in The Gilded Age , what everyone wanted to look like was the most successful person on earth. And a lot of the palaces they built, the clothes they wore, the things they did, were all designed to frame and exaggerate their success. I suppose we remind people [of that],” says Fellowes, who also created Downton Abbey . “After all, it is The Gilded Age ; it’s not The Golden Age. And “gilded” means there is an element of falseness that you’re trying to make something look better than it is, and that’s exactly what they were trying to do.” Peggy’s journey is not false, but rarified for any woman, especially for a Black woman of the time. Everything seems to be going Peggy’s way — personally and professionally. As she prepares for her wedding to Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), her once contentious soon-to-be mother-in-law Mrs. Kirkland (Phylicia Rashad) has become quite agreeable, even helping to plan the wedding, buying the wedding dress, and inviting her and her mother Dorothy Scott (Audra McDonald), whom she sparred with just last season, to join her “ladies club.” Not only has Peggy’s book Friends in These Times been published, publisher Ada and good friend Marian, she later beams to Agnes, is “talking about a lecture tour.” And her fiancé William, she brags when Ada asks, “is right behind me, urging me on at every step.” Peggy just couldn’t be happier. “She’s sort of undeniable in her Renaissance Woman era, which is exciting,” Denée Benton observed of her character this season. Judging by the first episode, Marian doesn’t fare too well this season. Caught off guard by all the fun she had at her cousin Oscar’s naughty after-party for his and Enid’s wedding at the very type of “establishment of ill-repute” she ended her engagement to Larry Russell (Harry Richardson) for attending last season , Marian, or Ms. Brook rather, stumbles greatly. Caught in a storm that results in Larry’s carriage being grounded, Marian finds herself in a hotel with Larry. Although they both have their own rooms, Larry knocks on her door and sweet talks his way in. Intoxicated by the air of freedom, Marian makes the one mistake her aunts Ada and Agnes had warned her against since the first day she showed up on their doorstep. And, once the sun comes up, the weight of losing her sexual purity fully hits her hard. By today’s standards and customs, especially since she and Larry are clearly in love, Marian’s horror may seem overblown. But Louisa Jacobson in later conversation with THR alongside her co-stars Denée Benton, Harry Richardson and Ben Ahlers reaffirms just how serious the situation truly is. “Marian is the person who reminds us of the way that things were then,” she says. “We have to remember what time period we’re living in — this is the 19 th century! Having premarital sex was the biggest cardinal sin.” That decision, she further explains, could absolutely cost Marian everything. “There’s an external obstacle,” Jacobson says “If people were to find out what happened in episode one between the two of them, she would be put out on the streets; she would be destitute; she would lose marriage prospects; her life would be completely ruined. And that is real. “And that is really hard to understand as a 2026 audience with all the freedoms that we have, and bodily autonomy that we hopefully still have,” she continues. “I think it’s more about there’s an external obstacle there, and there’s the internal obstacle of shame that has been baked in and really internalized due to decades and decades of women learning like these sort of Victorian purity and moral ideals that women were held to. So I think it becomes less about Larry and love, and more about how to navigate those waters and those obstacles.” As time stamped as Marian’s situation appears, The Gilded Age ’s appeal lies in its ability to resonate with today’s sensibilities. That Fellowes says has more to do with human nature. “At the basis of any drama series, you have to remember that human beings don’t change much. And so things that were worrying people in 1500 are probably still with us. You know nobody’s got enough money, and did they marry the right person, and why did their children do what they’re told anymore? You can find all of that in Socrates. And you know it’s still with us. I always hesitate to claim a message. You know, Sam Goldman, if you want to send a message, go to Western Union, and I slightly agree with that. But I do think that it’s good for people to realize that what they’re going through is not unique to them, or because they’re unusually cursed, or whatever it is. But in fact, it’s just part of being alive, and I think that in that way you can make a period drama feel modern because so much of what they’re going through is modern,” Fellowes says. Warfield agrees: “Period dramas are both timely and timeless because they deal with the fragility of you know the human experience. Of course, ours happens to be set in the Gilded Age, and we’re living through another Gilded Age, so history rhymes.” And those miss-if-you-blink cameos by David Letterman and Matt Damon don’t hurt either. *** New episodes of The Gilded Age drop every Sunday at 6 p.m. PT/9 p.m. ET on HBO until Dec. 20. title: ‘KPop Demon Hunters’ Directors Board Animated Short ‘Living With a Visionary’ as Exec Producers (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 9, 2026 11:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Living With a Visionary' Courtesy of The New York Times Op-Docs KPop Demon Hunters directors and Oscar winners Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans have boarded the award-winning animated short film Living With a Visionary as executive producers. Narrated by James Cromwell, the documentary, written, directed and animated by Stephen P. Neary, is a reflection on a poet’s 50-year marriage to an art curator grappling with Parkinson’s. The news comes before The New York Times Op-Docs will premiere the short this week. Living With a Visionary recently won the grand jury award for animation at AFI Fest after earlier this year being honored with the short film jury award for animation at the Sundance Film Festival. Related Stories Oscars 2027: Int'l Films in Focus 'Shame and Money' Director Explains Why His Int'l Oscar Hopeful About Dignity Feels So Physical Music Carly Rae Jepsen Set to Host 2027 Juno Awards The film, an adaptation of John Matthias’ memoir of the same name, explores the “bittersweet reflection on John’s relationship with his beloved wife Diana, and how it is transformed by the effects of her Parkinson’s treatment,” reads a synopsis. “As Diana’s medication besets her with vivid, often beautiful hallucinations, John, now her caregiver, adapts to her imaginary world.” Produced by Neary and Mireia Vilanova, the film consists of thousands of drawings, illustrated by hand on intersecting layers of vellum. The creator drew them over the course of three years at nights and on weekends while working full-time as a story artist and teaching classes at the California Institute of the Arts. Neary is known as the creator and showrunner of The Fungies! on Cartoon Network and HBO Max and the supervising producer on the Annie-nominated show Clarence . As a story artist, his credits include KPop Demon Hunters , The Super Mario Galaxy Movie , Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs , Rio and The Peanuts Movie . Living With a Visionary Courtesy of The New York Times Op-Docs “Somehow while working full-time on KPop Demon Hunters and raising a family, Stephen found the time to make this heartbreaking, beautiful film,” said Kang. “I don’t know how he did it, and honestly I’m worried he doesn’t sleep enough, but we’re so excited for more audiences to see Living With a Visionary. The world needs unique stories in animation and often the most impactful ones come from the least expected places.” Appelhans shared: “Stephen’s film feels like a sketch of the human soul. This assembly of lines that somehow captures love, grief, hallucination and connection. I got to live inside Cromwell’s narration and experience the heartache of being alive alongside the enduring power of love. A truly special piece of documentary filmmaking.” Neary expressed his gratitude. “It means the world to have Maggie and Chris support this small film I spent years drawing on paper,” he said. “ KPop Demon Hunters and Living With a Visionary are, stylistically, worlds apart. But I believe there’s a throughline of raw, emotional honesty in both these works capable of bringing a needed catharsis to viewers from a place they least expect it — animation.” Living With a Visionary joins eight other films on Op-Docs’ 2026 slate that it sees as awards contenders, including The Revolution Against Death by Joshua Oppenheimer, The Tuners and A Wolf in the Suburbs . title: ABC Developing Police Procedural From ‘Government Cheese’ Co-Creator Aeysha Carr and Ramón Rodríguez
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Denise Petski Denise Petski Senior Managing Editor More Stories By Denise ‘Melania, The Series’ Gets Prime Video Release Date & Trailer Ella Langley, Tim McGraw, Miranda Lambert Among Performers For CMA Awards More Details Revealed About ‘Ellen DeGeneres Show’ EP Matthew Wright’s Sudden Death View All November 9, 2026 11:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Aeyesha Carr, Ramón Rodríguez Kevin Kwan/Nino Munoz EXCLUSIVE: Government Cheese co-creator Aeysha Carr and Ramón Rodríguez are teaming to develop an Oakland, CA-set police procedural at ABC. The Untitled Aeysha Project hails from Carr, Rodriguez’s Altura Productions and 20 th Television, where Rodriguez is under a first-look deal. Written and executive produced by Carr, the untitled drama is about an ultra-wealthy, four-time widow who decides to fund a state-of-the-art forensic science facility to help Oakland police solve their most brutal murders. Rodriguez executive produces via his Altura Productions under his first-look deal, along with 3 Arts’ Oly Obst. Altura’s Stephanie Dietz serves as co-executive producer. 20 th Television is the studio. Watch on Deadline Carr co-created the surrealist dramedy Government Cheese , starring David Oyelowo, which recently aired its first season on Apple TV.
