title: ‘Survivor 51’ Castoff Brady Booker on That “Toxicity” Comment, Starving Through Challenges and What It Means to Be a “Brodie”
full_text: Skip to main content By Terry Terrones Plus Icon Terry Terrones @terryterrones Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 10:39am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Eric Macksoud and Brady Booker on 'Survivor 51.' Robert Voets/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. Logo text Professional wrestler Brady brought plenty of energy, intensity and a whole lot of “brodies” to Survivor 51 , but his aggressive gameplay ultimately caught up with him at the merge. After a chaotic Tribal Council saw even his closest allies turn against him in a 9-4 vote on the Nov. 4 episode, the normally outspoken Brady left without saying a word. In his exit interview with The Hollywood Reporter below, Brady explains his unusually quiet departure, responds to Jelly’s harsh criticism of his behavior and reveals just how much the lack of food affected him physically and emotionally. Related Stories General News Trump Reflects on Republicans' Midterm Losses, Reacts to J.D. Vance's Own Analysis in '60 Minutes' Interview TV Chris Pratt Tapped for King of Comedy Award at 2026 Kids' Choice Awards *** Let’s start with your exit. You’re a pretty outgoing guy, so it was surprising to see you leave without saying a word. What was going through your mind at that moment? I figured I was going to get some votes, but when I got to about six, I started to “read the room.” When Jeff [Probst, host] reads that last vote, it’s like a flash bang goes off. Everything just went “Eek!” and my soul left my body. When I do something brodie, I do it 110 percent. I’m balls to the wall. And when the competition ends, when that weight falls off you, you almost go back to being a regular person. I know that’s tough for people to believe. I do always have this energy, but man, it’s a different animal when I’m competing. I’ve done it at a high level with high intensity. I find that chaos fun, which is maybe why I tried to turn the game into a little bit of chaos myself. But me walking out and not saying anything was that quick thought of, “Do I blow up the game?” And that’s not how I would want it to be played. Now it’s my job to be on the jury. AAs I’m walking up there, you realize the surreal moment of what you’re going through. Only so many people have actually got to go through that. I took it all in — took in Jeff’s beautiful face one last time — and then I took my walk. Maggie, Kilby and Kristin all seemed to be firmly in your corner, yet all three voted against you. Did you see any signs they might turn on you, or did those votes completely blindside you? No, because I was worried about Kristin from the jump once Mike blew that all up. She wanted to believe me, but then I guess as it came closer to tribal and people started to hear numbers; she just ended up believing what the numbers were at. Kilby was advocating for me during tribal. But with the drama he had with Eric and him not wanting to write his name down again because I guess that’s the other option, he was looking out for his game. Then Carter and Lewis, both their names were getting thrown out. I guess that wasn’t shown as much, but they were also worried about themselves. So I appreciate them riding or dying for your boy. But no one’s pulling me aside telling me it’s the vote. No one came up to me and said, “It’s you.” And then with Thien An, she was a ride or die. Same thing with her. She never told me. I wish I would’ve prioritized that relationship a little bit more because of Thien An being so smart and being a ride or die. That’s something I may have overlooked. I truly didn’t have a number one. I was bouncing back and forth. At first, I thought it’d be Dev publicly, and then I thought it’d be Kilby because once the cool kids and the nerds split up, I thought I was going nerd side. I knew I couldn’t fit in with the cool kids. This personality, I get it. brodies are either going to love or hate me, but all I’m trying to do is elicit that reaction, so I get it and have fun doing it. I was going to Kilby, but then Kilby puts his foot in his mouth saying that stuff, and they were feeding me that he was a bad guy. I think Dev’s my number one, but in reality, Dev never was working with me because they had that previous alliance on the beach of their five that they prioritized over everything. And then thinking Maggie could be my number one when we find the boat together, but Maggie’s so frantic and we butt heads like a mom and son. Speaking of Maggie, your relationship with her was interesting. You trusted her with your extra vote and you were clearly working together, but you also seemed to be in conflict at times. Was the dynamic between you two, as you said, mother-son. Definitely. And after that first tribal where I got blindsided and I thought she was on my side. After the extra vote, Maggie saw a little bit of spice in me when I was a bulldozer or whatever, and that’s just me. When the stress is up, the intensity is up. I may be at two and they think I’m at a 10. So that’s where me and Maggie’s relationship fell there. I was a little too much brodie for her, and I get it. I love Maggie as a human being. She’s a fun player. It’s sad that she thinks I’m out here leaking everything because Dev actually walked up to me and Carter and was like, “Hey, are we going to tie Mike into this vote?” And that’s when we went over and told Mike. So great gameplay move by Dev; just further proves that Dev never really gave a crap about your brodie. I mean, dude’s great at playing to someone’s emotions. I bought into it. He’s an actor. Good for him. Unfortunately, Mike, we had this issue at Toka 2.0 that I wasn’t really caught up on. I figured we had such a good relationship that he would bring that up to me. I’m a pretty outspoken, say whatever you want, dog. We can talk. And it seems like he’s just not that type of guy. Misread that. I was actually the only person filling him in on 2.0 Beach. He would’ve got no other information. Before Patt got voted out, you would see Mike attached to Patt’s hip. You’d see them joke around, talk around, getting intimate and intricate information. But with me he would have very bland talks, very business, small talk, move on, very bland, boring. So I guess I’m glad that I could give him a little bit of personality, get him all spiced up and fired up at me. But all I was trying to do was keep brodie involved in the game. You and Kilby had mentioned at the start, right after the merge, that Mike was the person you were going to target. If he hadn’t won immunity, do you think the roles would be reversed and he’d be out and you’d still be in the game? Oh, 100 percent. If Mike doesn’t turn on me there, I still may be trying to be like, “Well, are you sure Mike?” Maybe a bigger threat or maybe Eric, because he’s someone’s extra number. And that’s when I probably should have refocused. The Kristin vote was getting thrown out there and it was only out there because everyone’s deathly afraid of her. She’s Moby Dick and we got to all team up to be Captain Ahab. I’ve never seen a more prepared, strategic, even keel player. If I got on the beach with Kristin day one, that’s who I would’ve died on that beach to make my number one. I knew after her making relationships with other people coming to us, she’s awesome. I knew how much I loved her then. Jelly had some pretty harsh words about you, saying you brought “a level of toxicity to this game that no one needs” and were always trying to take control. Did you have any idea she felt that way, and what’s your reaction to hearing that now? No, absolutely not. I mean, she’s bitter for some reason, but she was bitter with me from episode one. She always thought I was a big dumb jock. I’m not surprised. She was so bitter, but I never did anything to her to make her feel that type of way and control her game. I guess the only person I could understand that from is Mike or maybe even Maggie because I’m like, “Hey, let me dictate this.” But that was never the notion or ever had any malice or stuff like that. I don’t think there’s toxicity. I think I’m reactive. I’m passionate, and I think that I was totally misunderstood by Jelly, but that’s because she spends her time in a sociology professor’s office and not in a ring and not on the field and not in my neck of the woods. I recently spoke with Kamilla Karthigesu on my Next Time on…Survivor podcast, and she mentioned that bigger guys like David Kinne and Jonathan Young seemed to struggle more with the lack of food. Given your size, how much did hunger affect you out there, and do you think it influenced how you interacted with other players? It affects everybody, but my God, brodie, hell yes, does it affect me. When we were in those challenges, I’d flip a switch. I’d find that competitor in me and I’d dig deep, and that’s where all that intensity and passion and emotion comes from, because you got to dig deep to really perform and push yourself on nothing. When we finished that one where Mike shot the hoop and everyone’s running to get in there, I grabbed onto the floatie because I thought I was going to drown. I was so out of breath. When he [ Jeff Probst ] brought us to the merge feast and he’s like, “Hey, you’re going to have to earn it.” I didn’t have it anymore. I was passing out. I’d stand up too soon. I’d go back down. I’d be in the middle of a conversation. I’d find myself sleeping. I’m like, “What the heck’s going on?” So I mean, I was running on fumes and all that emotion and passion. Before I let you go, we need to settle something. Give me your definition of “brodie.” It’s an endearing term. It’s a welcoming term. I’m terrible with names. When I was in college, when the brodies come over, when we go to the bars, “Brodies going to the bars, going to the club!” It’s just me having a good time, having camaraderie between people. It’s a little bit more personal. It’s inviting. When I went to WWE, there’s 110 people with 10 different names and I can barely remember 10 names. So I just started “brodie,” and then if some of the chicks didn’t want to be called brodie, “Hey, what up, brodette.” It helped me just keep a good repertoire with people without having to get their name wrong because people get real offended by that. Listen, you can call me Brady, brodie,or dumbass. Just don’t call me before 8 a.m. It’s just a real good way to connect with people. So if you got a problem with that? Then, man, you don’t have enough problems. *** Survivor airs new episodes Wednesday at 8 p.m. on CBS , streaming on Paramount+. THR

title: Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi, Dies at 92
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 10:38am PT Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi, Dies at 92 By Jordan Moreau Plus Icon Jordan Moreau Latest Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi, Dies at 92 33 minutes ago Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Stomps to $6.7 Million in Previews 3 days ago Kimmarie Johnson, ‘Beverly Hills, 90210’ Actress and Miss USA Contestant, Dies at 50 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images for Turner Donnie Dunagan , who provided the original voice of Disney’s Bambi , died Wednesday, Nov. 4, of lung cancer, his agents confirmed to Variety . He was 92. “We were proud to represent a Marine, beloved by fans around the world for his roles in ‘Bambi’ and ‘Son of Frankenstein,'” his agents Kris Jones and Nery Lemus of CelebWorx told Variety . “While he asked us (in his words) ‘not to be sad due to the great life I lived,’ it would be amiss not to share the impact that Donnie had on people when they met him. His love for life was shown through his encouragement. He knew how to inspire and inspired us to be the best we could be. He had an infectious smile, a warmth and charisma that never shook the child-like spirit of his acting youth. He rallied other veterans, loved his fans, and above all else, loved his wife. We will always love you Donnie. You were the best of us.” Related Stories Hulu’s ‘The Circle’ Revival Sets SiriusXM’s Tinx as Host (EXCLUSIVE) Dunagan was born August 16, 1934, in San Antonio, Texas, but his family soon moved to Hollywood after a talent agent scouted him when he was three years old. He made his film debut in “Mary Carey’s Chickens” in 1938 and then played Peter von Frankenstein in 1939’s “Son of Frankenstein” (the grandson of the original mad scientist turned monster creator). He also appeared in “The Forgotten Woman” (1939), “Tower of London” (1939), “Vigil in the Night” (1940) and “Meet the Chump” (1941). In 1942, he voiced young Bambi’s in Disney’s beloved animated movie. After “Bambi,” Dunagan enlisted in the U.S. Marines and became the youngest drill sergeants in Corps history. He served three tours in Vietnam and retired as a major in 1977. For his service, he received a Bronze Star and three Purple Hearts. title: ‘Shame and Money’ Director Explains Why His Int’l Oscar Hopeful About Dignity Feels So Physical
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 9, 2026 10:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Astrit Kabashi (left) and Flonja Kodheli in 'Shame and Money.' Courtesy of Janis Mazuch After losing their livelihood in a village, a family in Kosovo is forced to move to the capital, Pristina. But the family struggles “in pursuit of a place in a hyper-capitalist society.” This brief description for director Visar Morina’s ( Exile , Babai ) Shame and Money just teases some of the stresses and challenges its characters face amid a high cost of living. The drama had its world premiere at the Sundance Film Festival, where it won the World Cinema Dramatic Grand Jury Prize. The award qualifies the film to compete for the best international feature film Oscar under the updated Academy rules. The cast is led by Astrit Kabashi and Flonja Kodheli and also features Kumrije Hoxa, Fiona Gllavica and Alban Ukaj. Related Stories Movies Think You'd Never Be a Cult Member or Get Manipulated? 'Father's House' Wants You to Think Again. TV 'The Other Elliot Sister' Greenlit at BritBox With Launch of Austen Anthology Franchise (Exclusive) Morina co-wrote the script for the vicky bane and Schuldenberg Films production with Doruntina Basha. Janis Mazuch was the cinematographer, while Joëlle Alexis was the editor. The producers are Fabian Altenried, Sophie Ahrens, Kristof Gerega, Pia Hellenthal and Morina. Oscilloscope Laboratories acquired North American distribution rights and is planning to release the movie in early 2027. THR ‘s review called Shame and Money “a tense and crushing view of the global economy through the eyes of a farmer in Kosovo.” The Sundance jury lauded the director for “his powerful and unique portrayal of human dignity in contemporary Kosovo that universally resonates,” calling Morina “a sensitive filmmaker who masterfully draws the audience into the daily struggles of a family [and who has] deep empathy for his characters.” Morina talked to THR about Shame and Money , which is his third film contending for the best international Oscar after Babai and Exile , and how it tells a story that resonates beyond Kosovo – and not only because the film shows a statue of Bill Clinton, which was erected because, as U.S. President, he led the 1999 NATO bombing campaign against what was then Yugoslavia, which forced the security forces of Yugoslav president Slobodan Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo. What was the inspiration for Shame and Money ? I shot my previous film, Exile , in Cologne. Flonja and Astrit, who are now the leads, had a tiny scene together. After the shoot, I took a picture of them, and they were standing next to each other. And when I was looking at it, it somehow reminded me of my parents. I kept going back to this image, and then Corona started, and I was thinking a lot about my parents and also worried about them. They live near Stuttgart. And somehow this image and the fact that I was worried about them got me to a point where I started to think of them less as my parents, and more as two random people being deeply influenced by politics, in their case because of Milošević. They are pawns of politics, which they don’t understand. But they have to deal with the consequences. So, the starting point was to think about how it would be if they left home now and not 30 or more years ago. Did you know the village where the family lives at the start of Shame and Money ? I actually wrote about the village I grew up in. I even wrote the film for the house in which I grew up. But it has not been used for 20 years, and it was in such a different shape. In the end, we decided to film it somewhere else. But there are actually two shots in my village. Did you focus on the universal experience that the local story, which you are telling, is reflecting today amid a cost of living crisis in many countries? I was very much focused on making the story as local as possible. And I truly believe that if I do a good job, there is no way that other people won’t find themselves in those stories and in those things. I wanted to have the actual numbers, such as the price of peppers, rent, salary – the real numbers at the time we were shooting. How do you think about life in Kosovo as being similar or different from other parts of the world? Kosovo has gone through so many very different phases and so many breaks. In Germany [where I live], for example, people are so used to many structures that they don’t even think about them. But in Kosovo, everything is so new, and you see the structures rebuilding themselves. Basically, you see society trying to make sense of all these changes. You feel like you are in a lab watching a society form itself. Tell me a bit about how you arrived at the title Shame and Money … I went to Kosovo for research, exploring the housing and job market, and spoke to people who were looking for both. Alongside the existential hardship driving these people, there was another force present: shame in front of others and shame in front of oneself. “Even your own mother doesn’t love you if you are broke,” said one man who was working as a day laborer. He sounded embarrassed when he said it. In Albanian, this sounds much harsher and more direct, describing someone who has just realized that even a mother’s love has a price. That sounds scary! This was something I thought was horrifying. But at the same time, I think there is a very strong connection between money and depression. I believe it is impossible to sustain a relatively healthy self – whatever that self may be – if you are constantly forced to prove your worth to others and, even worse, to yourself. If you have to demonstrate again and again that you are capable, that you deserve to belong, that you are something, that you can do something. This inevitably leads to exhaustion and depression. I did come away with a sense that the film was very much about humiliation versus… That was actually a very, very important part. In the end, if I break everything down, it’s a question of dignity. And that’s why we also focused on showing cows and other animals with dignity, and the work people are doing with dignity – everything. As a filmmaker, I can connect to this very much. If every day you put yourself on a street or wherever to find work, trying to convince others that you are worth being a part of it and that you are worth being seen, that you should be accepted, you get demoralized. As a visual and overall experience, Shame and Money made me feel quite exhausted, very much like your main characters. Did you do anything special to make the experience so physical and intense? That was basically the point – the physical experience. It was important not to put the characters on display, not to look down on them, [but] to take them seriously, and to put ourselves in their shoes as much as possible. They become poor, and poverty can also be portrayed in a very voyeuristic way. That’s why it was important to take the work they do seriously. So we were very keen on making any work shown be done as you would usually do it. When we didn’t know how to do something, we asked experts. Do you have any examples or so? For example, I learned what it takes to bring a person from a wheelchair to the bed. You have to make sure that the sheet is very straight; otherwise, it will get complicated and difficult for the skin. And you use your legs as a brake so he does not fall. There are all these tiny things. And that exhausts the actors. The effect of this was that it made the actors so focused on how they do things and move that their lines just came out. Their focus was less on how to say things or how to act and more on how to get this thing done. What does qualifying for the international Oscar category mean for the film and you? Oh, I´m excited. Hopefully, more people will see it. I’m also very glad that people praise the acting very much. So, yes, hopefully this will help with getting the film released in more places, and hopefully more people will watch it. THR

title: Julianne Moore, Josh Brolin and Daisy Ridley Lead the Buzziest Titles at AFM
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 9, 2026 10:00am Published on November 9, 2026 (L to R): Stars with projects looking for buyers at AFM 2026: Patrick Schwarzenegger, Daisy Ridley, Josh Brolin, Renée Zellweger, LaKeith Stanfield, Julianne Moore Getty The American Film Market’s 47th edition, taking place Nov. 10-15 at the Fairmont Century Plaza, AMC Century City and The Pavilion in Los Angeles, arrives at a moment of near-total disruption for the independent film business. The models that have long underpinned financing, production and distribution are in flux, squeezed by consolidation, changing audience habits and a market in which the traditional routes to getting a film made and seen are no longer a given. But the upheaval is also opening doors. A new generation of online creators-turned-filmmakers — Curry “Obsession” Barker, Kane “Backrooms” Parson and Mark “Iron Lung” Fischbach among them — is proving that audiences can be built outside the traditional system and carried onto screens. “Oddly, every independent success is still seen as a fluke, or gets put in a bucket,” says Jackie Brenneman, the new head of IFTA, which runs AFM. “What’s not being seen is that almost none of these films should have happened, because the structure of the business doesn’t support independent film. That they’ve broken through the way they have is just the tip of the iceberg of demand. Once we build the infrastructure to connect audiences with the stories they want across all different screens, the numbers are going to be much bigger.” That sense of untapped demand is echoed by international sellers, some of whom are returning to the market after time away. Among them is South Korea’s Finecut, back at AFM after several years with the animated feature Long Long Night , from Korean director Kyu Bock Youm, which follows a rhino and a penguin as they journey across the wilderness together. “As one of the last markets of the year, AFM is an important opportunity to introduce titles launched after Cannes to buyers, particularly for North and Latin America,” says Finecut sales manager JD Kim. “Considering the trajectory from Parasite to K-Pop Demon Hunters , I believe global interest in Korean culture and content remains strong.” THR ’s 2026 Hot List of the titles generating buzz at AFM spans star-led packages, international genre plays, animation, prestige dramas and films at various stages of production. The common thread is a search for projects — and business models — that can find their audience in a rapidly changing independent landscape. ‘Almost You’ Image Credit: Lisa O'CONNOR / AFP, Gareth Cattermole, Stephanie Augello Almost You DIRECTOR Matt Lipsey STARS Juno Temple, Joey King, James McAvoy BUZZ AI and grief collide in this high-concept tale about a robotics engineer mourning her younger sister, who feeds years of messages, videos and social media posts into an AI replica of her. The invention brings comfort — at first — before forcing her to confront a thorny question: if you could bring someone back, should you? A trio of Temple, King and McAvoy gives the timely premise some marquee value for buyers. SALES Bankside Films, UTA ‘ A Speck in the Sea ‘ Image Credit: Daniele Venturelli/WireImage, Katie FLORES / AFP A Speck in the Sea DIRECTOR Orlando Von Einsiedel STARS Josh Brolin, Jeremy Renner BUZZ Oscar-winning documentarian Von Einsiedel (The White Helmets) makes his fiction debut with this based-on-a-true survival tale of Johnny Aldridge (Brolin), a Montauk lobster fisherman who falls off his fishing boat in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean in the dead of night, with his best friend Anthony Sosinski (Renner), asleep below deck. ‘Breakwater’ Image Credit: Daniele Venturelli, Mike Marsland/WireImage Breakwater DIRECTOR Luc Walpoth STARS Olga Kurylenko, Alex Pettyfer BUZZ Action thrillers are a go-to at any AFM, which bodes well for this neo-noir project, about a woman trapped in a toxic marriage (Kurylenko) whose plan to blackmail her rich sadistic husband (Pettyfer) goes horribly wrong, landing her and her accomplice in a fight for survival on the high seas. SALES WestEnd Films ‘Control’ Image Credit: Stefania D'Alessandro, Gareth Cattermole Control DIRECTOR Robert Schwentke STARS James McAvoy, Julianne Moore BUZZ One of the higher-profile star-driven actioners on offer at AFM, this feature, from the director of Red, features McAvoy as a man who wakes up one morning with an untraceable device planted in his head and must follow a mysterious voice’s instructions or devastating consequences. SALES Studiocanal ‘Darlington’ Image Credit: Gareth Cattermole, Dia Dipasupil, Manoli Figetakis Darlington DIRECTOR Sascha Gervasi STARS Renée Zellweger, Dominic Sessa, Peter Dinklage BUZZ Zellweger plays a faded television actress invited to reprise her most famous role — only this time in the real world. Her host (Sessa) is a reclusive tech billionaire who has restored an English country estate and lives there as if it were 1923. As she settles into his carefully controlled fantasy, the line between illusion and reality starts to blur. Alexander Payne is on board as executive producer, which should add some cachet to the package. SALES Rocket Science, CAA ‘The Face of Horror’ Image Credit: Paul Archuleta, Aurore Marechal The Face of Horror DIRECTOR Anna Biller STARS Jonah Hauer-King, Kristine Froseth, Leo Suter BUZZ Biller’s gothic horror takes its cue from Yotsuya Kaidan , Japan’s most famous ghost story and a cornerstone of Japanese horror, adapted more than 30 times, including by Takashi Miike as Over Your Dead Body in 2014. Set amid war and plague, the story follows a knight who kills a landowner, marries his daughter and vows to avenge the very crime he committed. When he betrays her, his wife returns from the grave to exact revenge, drawing his squire and her sister into the supernatural reckoning. SALES Embankment Films ‘Falcon’ Image Credit: Courtesy of @DR Falcon DIRECTOR Marco Bellocchio STARS Pierfrancesco Favino, Louis Garrel, Benedetta Cimatti, Barbara Ronchi, Valeria Bruni Tedeschi BUZZ Bellocchio turns his lens on the boardroom with this drama about Sergio Marchionne (Favino) and his bid to rescue Fiat from the brink of collapse. Framed as a financial thriller with a psychological edge, the film tracks Marchionne’s battles with General Motors and Chrysler and his mentorship of heir John Elkann (Garrel), while counting the personal cost of saving an industrial empire. SALES Rai Cinema International Distribution ‘Feed’ Image Credit: Courtesy of Getty Feed DIRECTOR Leslye Headland STAR Rosamund Pike BUZZ This new project, which Pike will also produce, could provide an injection of socially-conscious body horror in the vein of The Substance for indie buyers. Inspired by 2022 Finnish feature Hatching , it stars Pike as a Muminfluencer desperate to make her gymnast daughter an online sensation. But when she turns to a suspicious supplement to help her along, monstrous things begin to happen. SALES The Veterans, CAA Media Finance ‘Found Alive’ Image Credit: XYZ Films Found Alive DIRECTOR Carlota Pereda STARS Chloë Grace Moretz, Rupert Friend BUZZ Genre buyers get a festival-tested option here: the thriller opened the 2026 Sitges Film Festival ahead of its AFM outing. Ten years after escaping a sadistic captor, a young woman agrees to mentor a newly rescued survivor. When the girl’s story points to other missing victims, she is drawn into a deadly game of cat-and-mouse. The English-language debut of Piggy director Pereda is adapted from Carla Norton’s Edge of Normal book series. SALES XYZ Films; CAA Media Finance, XYZ Films ‘Get Rid of It’ Image Credit: Tiffany Rose, Lionel Hahn, Brianna Bryson Get Rid of It DIRECTOR Ry Russo-Young STARS Daisy Ridley, Sosie Bacon, Simon Rex BUZZ A one-night stand leaves Harper with something unexpected growing inside her in this horror thriller, which sends her and her estranged sister on a desperate search for medical help. With the man from the encounter, religious fanatics and, eventually, the FBI all in pursuit, the sisters must confront both the creature and the wounds that drove them apart. The film is scheduled to shoot in February 2027. SALES Upgrade, CAA Media Finance, Range Select ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Image Credit: AGC Marketing Gods Don’t Give Gifts DIRECTOR Zack London STARS Richard Cotton, Sam Dale, Ben Kersley BUZZ Add another name to the roster of online creators making the leap to features: YouTuber Zack London ( Gossip Goblin) makes his debut with this animated sci-fi horror anthology, set in a future where transhumanism has pushed humanity far beyond recognition. Across four stories, ordinary people turn to strange new technologies to satisfy primal urges, exposing a widening rift between body and mind. SALES AGC Studios ‘It’s Alright’ Image Credit: Paras Griffin, Mike Marsland It’s Alright DIRECTOR Scott Stewart STARS Paul Bettany, Asha Banks, Colin Firth, Gugu Mbatha-Raw BUZZ A Brit feel-good comedy with a strong music hook, this feature from Legion and Dark Skies director Stewart sees Bettany playing an aging rock star, with real-life pop singer Banks as his estranged daughter, an aspriring singer-songwriter. With a score produced by Marius de Vries, music producer on La La Land , CODA and Moulin Rouge!, this package should have AFM buyers humming along. SALES Protagonist Pictures, CAA Media Finance ‘I’m With Stupid’ Image Credit: Jenna Berman, Alexandra Carillo-Vaccino, Oriana Layendecker I’m With Stupid DIRECTOR Hannah Pearl Utt STARS Jacob Tremblay, Kate McKinnon, Ego Nwodim, Chabely Ponce BUZZ A teen comedy about two slackers at the opposite ends of their high school’s social spectrum forced to work together to try and graduate. With few mainstream comedies on offer in the market, this could be the one to get buyers to open up. SALES Upgrade, UTA Independent Film Group, After Hours ‘In Her Shadow’ Image Credit: Paras Griffin/Getty Images for ESSENCE In Her Shadow DIRECTOR Rowan Athale STARS Letitia Wright BUZZ This supernatural horror thriller sees Black Panther: Wakanda Forever star Wright playing Annie Cutter, a celebrated author who adopts the daughter of her estranged, recently-deceased sister, a girl her sister kept locked in a basement for five years. But after taking the girl in, Cutter begins to suspect her sister may have had a reason to be afraid of the child. SALES Bankside Films ‘The Journeyman’ Image Credit: John Parra, Francois G. Durand The Journeyman DIRECTOR Ángel Manuel Soto STARS Patrick Schwarzenegger, Leslie Grace BUZZ Blue Beetle director Soto pivots to sports-crime with this story of a down-on-his-luck tennis pro who is drawn into the dark world of match-fixing as he tries to make ends meet for his family. Schwarzenegger and Grace lead the cast. SALES AGC Studios, WME, UTA ‘The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd’ Image Credit: Benoit Soler The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd DIRECTOR Tim Blake Nelson STARS Amanda Seyfried, Scoot McNairy BUZZ Based on true events, this drama, which premiered to strong reviews in Toronto , follows an English teacher trapped in an abusive marriage who takes a job at a maximum-security prison in Oklahoma and falls for a charismatic inmate who is also a student in her class. SALES WestEnd Films ‘ Mare Nostrum ‘ Image Credit: Courtesy of HanWay Mare Nostrum DIRECTORS Mariano Cohn and Gastón Duprat STAR Antonio Banderas BUZZ This feature, from the Argentine directors of Official Competition (2021) should have potential beyond the Spanish-language market. Banderas stars as a container ship captain who takes on a boat of African migrants, only to land in a political storm when he tries to dock in Europe. SALES HanWay ‘The Portrait’ Image Credit: Samir Hussein, Michael Loccisano The Portrait DIRECTOR Sarah Colangelo STARS Gillian Anderson, Rebecca Hall BUZZ A pitch for a more adult demographic, this new project from Colangelo, director of The Kindergarten Teacher (2018) is billed as a Hitchcockian thriller about an acclaimed writer (Anderson) who for years has been having an affair with a married man. When he is struck ill and she can’t see him anymore, the writer commissions his artist wife (Hall), to paint her portrait, setting up a showdown between the two women. SALES Rocket Science, WME ‘Safe Space’ Image Credit: Lisa O'CONNOR / AFP, Aurore Marechal Safe Space DIRECTOR Gillian Wallace Horvat STARS Joey King, LaKeith Stanfield BUZZ Dating is hard enough without an alien. In this high-concept sci-fi comedy from I Blame Society director Horvat, an intelligent but insecure scientist escapes a toxic relationship with a co-worker, only to rebound into what may be the most toxic relationship in the galaxy: an affair with a gorgeous alien. SALES Lucky Number, WME, CAA ‘Speed The Plow’ Image Credit: David Livingston/Getty Images Speed the Plow DIRECTOR David Mamet STARS Anthony Mackie, Sharon Stone, Ben Mendelsohn, Emily Alyn Lind BUZZ Hollywood inside baseball from Mamet, who revisits the town’s power games in this black comedy about a newly appointed studio chief offered a guaranteed blockbuster — or an important art-house film championed by his office temp. The choice becomes a test of professional ambition and personal integrity. SALES The Solution Entertainment Group ‘Untitled Armando Iannucci Package’ Image Credit: Jeff Kravitz/FilmMagic Untitled Armando Iannucci Package DIRECTOR Armando Iannucci STARS Taron Egerton, Alicia Vikander, James McAvoy BUZZ The award-winning writer/director of Veep and The Death of Stalin is trying his hand at the conspiracy thriller in this hot project. Plot details are being kept under wraps but the A-list cast, and Iannucci’s pedigree, should bring buyers in. SALES FilmNation Entertainment, UTA Independent Film Group ‘Violet’ Image Credit: Amy Sussman, Kayla Oaddams, Taylor Hill Violet DIRECTOR Patrick Brice STARS Lili Reinhart, Danny Ramirez, Suki Waterhouse, Mark Duplass, Lukas Gage BUZZ A horror thriller with a tech edge, this feature from Creep director Brice follows a widower Sean (Ramirez) trying to move on after the death of his fiancée, Violet (Waterhouse). He finds new love with his childhood friend (Reinhart). But then Sean begins to receive unsettling text messages from someone, or something, claiming to be dead ex. someone, or something, claiming to be his dead ex. SALES FilmNation Entertainment THR

title: ‘Love Is Blind’ Star Rob Feeley Breaks His Silence on Michaella, the Beekeeper and Why He Nearly Skipped the Reunion
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 10:00am PT ‘Love Is Blind’ Star Rob Feeley Breaks His Silence on Michaella, the Beekeeper and Why He Nearly Skipped the Reunion By Clayton Davis Plus Icon Clayton Davis Chief Awards Editor byClaytonDavis Latest Oscar Predictions: Best Casting — ‘Being Heumann’ and ‘La Bola Negra’ Found the Year’s Boldest Discoveries. Will the Academy Reward Them? 21 hours ago Oscar Predictions: Production Design — Could Something as Innovative and Cool as ‘Backrooms’ Find Love? 2 days ago Jesse Eisenberg and Julianne Moore on ‘The Debut,’ Testing AI to ‘Make Sure It’s Bad’ and Hoping ‘Now You See Me 4’ Gets Made 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Netflix Rob Feeley is sitting in his car. He’s taking the Zoom call from the driver’s seat, two days before the “ Love Is Blind ” Season 11 reunion drops on Netflix — and almost two years following the night that turned him from fan favorite into the most talked-about man on the Boston edition of the dating series. He’s screened the reunion, and the first thing he wants to do is get one piece of internet lore straight. Related Stories Hulu’s ‘The Circle’ Revival Sets SiriusXM’s Tinx as Host (EXCLUSIVE) “I’m the Walmart Travis Kelce,” he jokes when asked if the Kansas City Chiefs tight end or Taylor Swift ever reached out about the resemblance that launched a thousand memes. “I’m a lot less athletic and I have a lot less money.” It’s the kind of self-deprecating line that made Feeley, a 40-year-old AI infrastructure salesperson, easy to root for in the pods. That’s where he fell for retail executive Michaella Giorgio and got engaged. But we saw something different at the reunion, as he was hunched forward on the couch with his elbows on his knees, waiting for a beating that never fully arrived. Michaella, as it turned out, saved most of her fire for beekeeper Matt Waldrip, whom she had quietly dated after filming. What did arrive this season was a reckoning. At the cast’s first get-together back in Boston, Feeley spiraled, going after Matt, dismissing the “experiment” and daring viewers to cancel him. Before that, a dinner with his five closest friends left Michaella sitting through a barrage of comments from one of them, his friend Jay. After all of it, the engagement didn’t survive. In his exclusive exit interview with Variety , Feeley alluded to a run of losses in the year before filming. Over the course of our conversation, he lays them out plainly: a long-term relationship ended, he lost his job, two of his best friends died and his father was in hospice. “I’m a human being just like all of us,” he says. “One of my worst moments was caught on Netflix.” Feeley also speaks about why he almost skipped the reunion, his 78-year-old mother who nearly flew across the country to sit in the audience and whether he’d ever do a dating show again. You were a fan favorite early in the season, and then you became the most discussed person on the show, all within a single episode. What was it like when you opened your phone after that episode aired? Man, I couldn’t even really watch it. This has been hanging over my head for a year and eight months. It was one of the toughest moments I’ve had, probably as a person. I watched it before it came out because I had to go film the reunion, but when it aired, I still had to perform at work and everything else. All the text messages, all the hate online. I’ve never really been through that. I got the internet chirps early on, when they first called me “mama’s boy” and “AI this.” But I knew this was going to be a different level. It was a hard time, to be completely honest. It still is. A lot of people were taken by the way you spoke about your mother and your father. I lost my dad in the last couple of years, too, so that connected with me. Looking back, was it too soon to put yourself in that kind of vulnerable position? I’m a person who bottles things in, and it wasn’t just my father. It’s not an excuse. I didn’t know they were going to post my exit interview, and I wasn’t trying to excuse my behavior by blaming it on losses. But subconsciously, I probably wasn’t in the right mental space. The sequence was kind of crazy. My long-term relationship broke up. I left the house. At the same time, I lost my job. Then my best friend passed away. Then my other best friend passed away. And then my father was in hospice. I’m trying to keep my head on straight, and I threw my name in the hat for “Love Is Blind.” I’d never watched the show in my life, to be completely frank. I just wanted to find love. I think all of those things poured onto me without me even knowing it. You tell yourself, “I’ll be OK. Keep moving. You’re a man. Keep moving. This is a good opportunity.” But I didn’t know what the whole thing entailed. No phones, sequestered, all of that. With my anxiety, it was a pressure cooker. There were nights in the hotel room by yourself where I’d talk to my dad. At the top of the reunion, you said you weren’t even going to come. How close were you to being a no-show? Out of respect for Michaella, I owed it to her to come and talk. She and I have talked since the show, but I felt like I couldn’t just leave her on an island. Whatever she had to say about how I behaved publicly, she deserved an explanation publicly. That was a big part of it. But who wants to go in front of America and be a punching bag? I was ready for it, though. Be a man in the night, be a man in the morning. Michaella deserved for me to go to the reunion. You mentioned going away for 50 days after everything came out. Was that a program, or did you seclude yourself? It wasn’t a program. I was depressed. You can ask my friends. I was full of anxiety. I didn’t go into my basement and seclude myself for 50 days. I just worked out, stayed away from a lot of things, didn’t go out, didn’t drink at all, ate right. And I sought counseling. A psychiatrist. I was like, “All right, I got to get this shit right.” I might have showed up to one place in those 50 days. I was very on my grind, focused on getting myself right mentally, because that was a very, very tough experience for me. You seemed grateful at the reunion that you’d made that change by going to therapy. I think it’s important for men to see men like you giving it the seal of approval. Are you still working at it? Absolutely. I just met with my psychiatrist last night. The one thing I’d tell people is, it’s not a two-day thing or a three-day thing. You can’t give up after two or three months. You have to continuously go. I’ve suffered from severe anxiety my whole life. When I was very young, my mom put me in counseling and the lady would be like, “Take your temperature and put it this way” and I felt like I could outsmart her. I had very bad separation anxiety with my mom and my little brother. My psychologist told me anxiety is just another word for fear. You fear the unknown. And that was a lot of what happened on “Love Is Blind.” If you’re going to go to therapy, don’t just go three times and knock it. It takes a long time to really get the treatment. I was surprised I didn’t see your mom at the reunion. Funny story. She’s 78. I bought a house this year and put my mom in the “in-law” apartment because her landlord was steamrolling her and raising her rent. So I still joke that I live with my mom. I have no ego. She was supposed to come to L.A. with my brother. I go downstairs to her apartment, and she’s got her clothes laid out on the bed, so cute and stressing out, like a kid going on vacation. She just wanted to support me. And I said, “Ma, if you’re doing this because you think I need you there, I appreciate it, but I can’t put you on a flight across the country to have anxiety.” And I’m happy I didn’t, because that taping was six hours. It would have been overwhelming for her. It wasn’t fair to my mother. God works in mysterious ways. My best friend came in her place with my brother. I think your mom might go down as one of the favorite parents in “Love Is Blind” history. The one thing is authenticity. She’s an authentic person. Let’s go back to “the dinner” with Michaella and your friends. What was it like watching that episode, and what were the conversations with your boys afterward? I wanted to bring five of my close friends because they’re super important to me. People asked why I didn’t bring women. I just wanted her to meet my close nucleus of friends. I didn’t know my one friend [Jay] was going to behave that way. I didn’t know he’d been drinking beforehand. Rewatching it was a complete embarrassment. I was ashamed. My friend is completely embarrassed. There’s no part of him that thinks that’s funny. In the moment, I didn’t know how severe it was. When I rewatched it, I was like, “What the fuck, jeez Louise.” Michaella didn’t deserve to sit there and listen to any of that BS. These are men of integrity. I know these guys are good people. If I could change it, I’d change it 100 out of 100 times. He and I had a serious, serious conversation. I can assure you he feels 10 times worse than I do. He’s still not back to himself. It’s affected us, it’s affected families. It’s not indicative of who we are. The one person I care about in that whole thing who had to listen to that BS is Michaella. I’ve apologized to her, and I continue to. And no excuses for Jay at all. But it might come out later, so I’ll say it. He’s also been battling stage three lung cancer. It was during that time, too. He’s in remission now, but I don’t know where his head was in that moment and it’s not excusable at all. I just know that right now he’s not in a good place. There’s no one more embarrassed than him and me about that scene. And obviously Michaella. It was tough to watch. Michaella said at the reunion that some of it came from your paranoia. You said it was the cameras. Do you feel like she will go down as “the one that got away?” It would have been great to meet in a different environment. I didn’t behave correctly under the pressure of it. I love who Michaella is. She’s an incredible human being. I think the world of her … still do. I told her I’m here for you whenever you need me, and I mean that. I told her, “You deserve better than me. There’s going to be someone who can do everything you want, and I apologize that it couldn’t be me.” Behind the pods, it was incredible. Then it got to the real world, and I thought, “Holy shit, this might happen.” And I folded. She didn’t deserve that. That’s the reality. I need to ask about “Beekeeper,” aka Matt. Michaella came for his throat the entire reunion but was very soft with you. What’s the story there? Post-show, a lot of the guys hung out. I learned that Michaella and Matt were seeing each other, maybe seven or eight months after the show. To be completely honest, it stung a little bit. No pun intended. (Laughs) You’re doing dad jokes now. Cam’s going to lose his brand. It stung naturally. But Michaella is a grown woman who can date whoever she wants, even if it’s someone from the cast. It’s not her duty to go date someone who’s not. My initial reaction was, “I hope they’re happy.” I didn’t know when they broke up. I wasn’t going to DM Michaella or poke Matt. It’s not my business. Then apparently shit went south. I think a lot of us were shocked. I didn’t know the Harry Potter stuff, the chicken cutlets. He was doubling down. He came off complimentary at first, and then I don’t know where it was going. I was just as surprised as you. That was an electric reunion, I’ll tell you that. John and Sarah were the season’s only married couple. What was your reaction to how their story played out in the end? Listen, there’s no room for infidelity in life. You pick your person. I don’t care if it’s on a TV show. You can’t behave that way. The bed you made, you got to lay in it. I try to mind my business as much as I can. Some of us knew about the text messages, the explicit things. The other things in their relationship, I frankly don’t know anything about. But you can’t text an escort or a stripper, whatever it was. He lost Sarah, so he paid the ultimate price. You don’t like to see anybody go through that hurt, and clearly Sarah was hurt. Families were involved, and it was getting ugly. Then John’s dad got involved. I think Maury is a fierce protector of friends and family. He dated Sarah in the pods, and I think he was protective of her. The father is protective of his son. It just unfolded in a crazy way. Everyone’s emotional, reactionary. My brother and my best friend were sitting right next to John’s dad, so they were in the thick of it. We were all kind of shell-shocked. Michaella’s fall at the reunion looked mortifying, but she took it like a champ. Is that just her personality? When we first met, she had these chattering teeth, like the yellow wind-up kind, because she likes to laugh. She’s self-deprecating like me. She takes things in stride. Life’s not that serious. If anything, it makes her relatable. She took a nice fall and she got up like, “Okay, then.” Michaella is very lighthearted, and that’s part of the reason I fell in love in the pods. I read body language. You’re a big presence; you take up space, but on that couch, you looked like you were in a cocoon, bracing for impact. Am I reading that right? First off, the chairs are super uncomfortable. I didn’t want to lean back and look like I was eating potato chips. My posture sucks to begin with. I’m trying not to bump into Blake on my left, trying to put the pillow under me. The easiest thing was to put my elbows on my knees. But yeah, I took it very seriously. I hurt somebody. It wasn’t a joke to me. I wasn’t coming in loose and busting chops. These are people’s lives. It’s Michaella’s life. I didn’t know what to expect. But try sitting where they had me for six hours. Where do you hope you and Michaella end up after this? Friends? I want her to live the best life ever and keep being a shining star. I think this will catapult her to doing great things. I’d like to be friends and be cordial. We gave each other a big hug after the reunion. I don’t know if they caught that. I texted her that night, like, “How did you take things? I know it was intense.” We did have something great. It was just in a really weird environment for me, and I wasn’t mentally prepared to be the person Michaella needed in that moment. Are you dating anyone? And would you do another dating show like “Perfect Match?” I might get kicked off before I even touch foot on the show. [Laughs] I’ve definitely learned a few things. But right now, I am seeing someone. So probably not. It’s not in my cards at the moment. So that’s a no to “Perfect Match” until further notice. Until further notice, that’s a no, my friend. Anything I didn’t ask that you want to say? First and foremost, I want to apologize to Michaella and not just Michaella. Anybody who was offended, anybody whose experience I ruined that night, I want to vehemently apologize. I’m a firm believer in growth. I’m a human being just like all of us, and one of my worst moments was caught on Netflix. I have an enormous friend group of great people in my community. I coach Pop Warner. I’ve worked hard to build my character and be there for people. I don’t want to let one bad moment define the person that I am. I hope some folks can give me grace. I don’t need people to feel bad for me, but I need people to understand that was one blip. I’m not blaming producers. It was my own behavior. I wish I could turn things back, and that’s not indicative of the man that I am. The “Love Is Blind” Season 11 reunion is now streaming on Netflix. title: Carly Rae Jepsen Set to Host 2027 Juno Awards
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All November 9, 2026 9:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The singer has released her ambitious 24-track double album 'Day and Night.' Mikayla LoBasso Canadian pop star Carly Rae Jepsen has been tapped to host the 56th annual Juno Awards next year. The singer-songwriter will also perform along with Angine de Poitrine, the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) said Monday. Jepsen, a three-time Juno winner, will host Canadian music’s biggest night for the first time on April 4, 2027, while Our Lady Peace will be inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, while also performing. Jepsen for the last 15 years has released a host of critically regarded pop songs. Her breakout hit “Call Me Maybe,” initially released in Canada in 2011, blew up across the world in 2012 and earned the singer two Grammy nominations and a spot atop the Billboard Hot 100. Related Stories Movies Think You'd Never Be a Cult Member or Get Manipulated? 'Father's House' Wants You to Think Again. TV 'The Other Elliot Sister' Greenlit at BritBox With Launch of Austen Anthology Franchise (Exclusive) That followed Jepsen placing third on Canadian Idol in 2007. Her second studio album, Kiss , won album of the year and pop album of the year at the 2013 Juno Awards, while also picking up the single of the year trophy. Jepsen has just released her latest project, Day and Night , a 24-track double album. The 2026 Juno Awards, Canada’s version of the Grammys, was hosted by Mae Martin and featured legendary folk singer and songwriter Joni Mitchell making a rare public appearance in Canada to receive a lifetime achievement award. Michael Bublé hosted the 2025 Juno Awards in his hometown of Vancouver. The 56th Annual JUNO Awards will air live on the CBC network and YouTube channel and is produced by Insight Productions. THR

title: James Gunn Speaks Out After Stepping Down at DC, Says It Had ‘Highest of Highs’ but ‘Has Been Trying’: ‘I Dislike the At-Times Corporate Nature of the Job’
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 9:56am PT James Gunn Speaks Out After Stepping Down at DC, Says It Had ‘Highest of Highs’ but ‘Has Been Trying’: ‘I Dislike the At-Times Corporate Nature of the Job’ By Jordan Moreau Plus Icon Jordan Moreau Latest Donnie Dunagan, Original Voice of Bambi, Dies at 92 59 minutes ago James Gunn Speaks Out After Stepping Down at DC, Says It Had ‘Highest of Highs’ but ‘Has Been Trying’: ‘I Dislike the At-Times Corporate Nature of the Job’ 2 hours ago Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Stomps to $6.7 Million in Previews 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images James Gunn has spoken out after he and Peter Safran were replaced by Jeremy Latcham as the head of DC Studios . In a surprising move on Monday, Skydance replaced Gunn and Safran with Marvel veteran Latcham as the president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. It ends Gunn and Safran’s four-year run as the heads of DC Studios, where they rebooted the superhero universe with “Superman,” “Supergirl,” “Clayface” and the HBO series “Lanterns.” Related Stories Hulu’s ‘The Circle’ Revival Sets SiriusXM’s Tinx as Host (EXCLUSIVE) Gunn, who is a frequent social media user and regularly chatted with fans on X and Threads, posted a lengthy statement after the news of his stepping down. He gave a shoutout to Safran and thanked the DC fans, but he also spoke out about the challenges of the job. “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years” View this post on Instagram Read his full statement below. Oh, boy. What a four years. Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios. When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job. There have been so many highs along the way – releasing Superman and Clayface, making Peacemaker, reading the scripts to The People Vs, the entire process of Man of Tomorrow, which thus far has been the best filmmaking experience of my life, and numerous other moments. The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran , the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend. But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head. So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and I are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on. Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen. title: ‘SNL’ Alums Bobby Moynihan, Aristotle Athari & Taran Killam Team On Collectibles Podcast ‘On Display’ – Watch The First Episode
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn & Peter Safran Out, Former Marvel Exec Jeremy Latcham In Read the full story By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Sinners’ Breakout Miles Caton Joins Denzel Washington Thriller At Amazon MGM/UA Aaron Paul To Play Music Mogul Jimmy Iovine In Universal’s ‘Snoop’; Giovanni Ribisi Also Set ‘SNL’ Alums Bobby Moynihan, Aristotle Athari & Taran Killam Team On Collectibles Podcast ‘On Display’ – Watch The First Episode View All November 9, 2026 9:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source EXCLUSIVE: Today, Saturday Night Live alumni Bobby Moynihan , Aristotle Athari and Taran Killam launched On Display , a new podcast birthed out of their shared passion for collectibles. The trio loves collecting everything from comic books to action figures and movie memorabilia. Each week on the podcast, they’ll be joined by a celebrity guest to talk about their cherished items and hobbies, while sharing their own personal fandoms. The show brings together comedy, nostalgia and often-heartfelt stories about personal obsessions, and what certain prized possessions really mean to both the hosts and their guests. Related Stories Late Night TV Milwaukee Brewers Make Surprise "Weekend Update" Appearance After World Series Win With Returning 'SNL' Alum Bobby Moynihan Podcast Comedians Leslie Liao & Jason Cheny Team With All Things Comedy On 'Happy Fun Times' Podcast On Display premiered today at 9 a.m. PT. New episodes will go out weekly on Mondays across YouTube and wherever else podcasts are found. The first season will feature 12 episodes, with five or six already shot. Watch a special preview above and the full first episode below. Watch on Deadline The pod is produced by StudioTen42 , in association with the comedian-owned podcast network All Things Comedy . Billy Rosenberg and Drew Eller are exec producing for ATC, alongside Guy Robinson for StudioTen42, and Andy Smith for high-end collectibles company, Sideshow , which is the show’s sponsor. Athari came to the idea for On Display after connecting with Andy Smith, who works in PR at Sideshow, during his time working on the film M3GAN 2.0 . Through Smith, he learned that Killam is a passionate collector who lost a collection he’d spent decades building — featuring some irreplaceable items — when his house burned down in the devastating Palisades Fire of January 2025. On Saturday Night Live for just one season, from 2021-2022, Athari hadn’t overlapped there with either Moynihan, who did nine seasons from 2008-2017, or Killam, who was on for six seasons from 2010-2016. After learning about what had happened to Killam, he began working with Sideshow to help him rebuild his collection. Then, he leaned that Moynihan is an avid collector, as well, leading to initial discussions amongst the trio about On Display . Killam told Deadline, “Hosting this podcast is beyond fun. Being a collector my entire life has directly informed what I do for a living. It’s been great interviewing other accomplished collectors and learning how it informs their own professional process. It’s also really great to see lots of really cool toys.” Moynihan commented, “I love talking about things I love with people I love while people who love things watch this thing we hope they love because we also love…it.” Athari added, for his part, “I feel immensely fortunate to share my affinity for collecting ephemera with friends and transform that shared passion into a creative and entertaining endeavor. Apparently, the only difference between collecting and hoarding is having a podcast.” Moynihan is repped by UTA, OPE Partners and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; Athari by CAA, Stride Management and Gang, Tyre Ramer; and Killam by UTA and Ziffren Brittenham. title: Pink Announces Sphere Residency, Becomes First Female Solo Headliner at Venue
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ethan Millman Plus Icon Ethan Millman Music Editor View All November 9, 2026 9:41am Add us as a Google Preferred Source P!NK Theo Wargo/Getty Images Pink is set for a nine-date residency at the Sphere in Las Vegas next year, the pop star announced on Monday, becoming the first female solo headliner at the high tech venue since it opened in 2023. “This idea has been bubbling up for years, and I finally get to share it with all of you,” Pink wrote on her social media on Monday. “Let’s celebrate! The highs, the lows, the new, the scary, the never been done before. For the first time, I’m giving a show a home and I hope you’ll visit. It’s my FIRST EVER residency. @spherevegas, 2027. I can’t wait to have you over.” Pink will open her residency on Wednesday, September 29, with subsequent shows on October 1 and 2, October 6, 8 and 9, October 27, 29, and a final show on October 30. Presale will begin on November 18 at 10 a.m. PST, with a general onsite starting at 10 a.m. on November 20th. Pink will become the first female solo act to headline the Sphere and just the second woman overall after the Gwen Stefani-fronted No Doubt played a residency of their own over the summer. She joins a list of stars including John Mayer, Rush, Carín León and Metallica all slated to play the Sphere next year. Her residency will mark Pink’s most notable concerts since she wrapped her Summer Carnival tour back in 2024. She hosted the Tony Awards over the summer and was just nominated for entrance into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. THR

title: ‘Gordon,’ a Big Netflix Series From Argentina, Unpacked by Pablo Trapero and Star Rodrigo de la Serna
full_text: × Nov 9, 2026 9:28am PT ‘Gordon,’ a Big Netflix Series From Argentina, Unpacked by Pablo Trapero and Star Rodrigo de la Serna A car thief turned Argentina Dirty War death squad member, torturer and ‘perverse psychopath,’ Gordon begs the question of how such a monster could have gained so much power in 1970s Argentina. The series answers that question By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest ‘Gordon,’ a Big Netflix Series From Argentina, Unpacked by Pablo Trapero and Star Rodrigo de la Serna 2 hours ago Sanfic Prizes: ‘Monguen’ and ‘Narciso’ Win at Pared-Back Ceremony Due to Sudden Demise of ‘A Fantastic Woman’ Director Sebastián Lelio 1 day ago Seville European Film Festival Honors Agnieszka Holland, Thierry Frémaux and Cartoon Saloon 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rodrigo de la Serna in 'Gordon' Credit: Marcos Ludevid 2025 A Netflix Nov. 18 bow, Pablo Trapero ’s “Gordon,” led by “Money Heist” star Rodrigo de la Serna , weighs in and is shaping up as Argentina’s series of the year. Set over 1970-76 and shot over seven months with large cinematographic ambition by two of Argentina’s greatest directors, Trapero (“Leonera,” “The Clan”) and Pablo Fendrik (“The Bronze Garden,” “Amongst Men”), “Gordon” lifts the lid on the real-life Ánibal Gordon – an infamous torturer, psychopath and sybarite of violence – and through him Argentina’s biggest horror story, its 1974-83 Dirty War. Related Stories Hulu’s ‘The Circle’ Revival Sets SiriusXM’s Tinx as Host (EXCLUSIVE) If periods of terror can have its icons, one of the War’s was Gordon who acts like a “sci-fi portal, opening doors to Argentina’s different universes of the time,” says Trapero. “Gordon,” a seven-part period psychological action thriller, marks the return of Trapero to his native Argentina after eight years. Unlike the famed international series he has co-directed of late, such as “ZeroZeroZero,” here Trapero also co-writes, with Marcos Osorio Vidal, a sign of his artistic investment in “Gordon.” It’s also a return to the near same time period and film noir-melodrama mix of 2016’s “The Clan,” Trapero’s best festival and commercial hit, a portrait of Argentina’s well-to-do Puccio family which kidnapped and murdered associates for money. Winning a best director Venice Silver Lion, “The Clan” went on to gross $20.4 million worldwide, rating as a blockbuster in Argentina. Hypnotic and nightmarish, “Gordon” first captures its protagonist, played memorably by De la Serna, in a car with his wife and infant son crossing Argentina’s huge grassy Pampa plain to a new home.He courteously greets an old man steering a cart and horse they pass, takes in a wounded puppy and later sipping tea from a porcelain teacup with a new neighbor, Dora, the widow of a Vice-Admiral. “You look like you have a military bearing. Were you in service?” Dora asks at the start of a series’ trailer. “No, no, I’m a simple businessman,” Gordon answers, but is obviously flattered. His gentlemanly charm is also, however, a mask. Cut in the trailer to Gordon and a gang checking revolvers for a robbery, then a torched getaway car aflame after a heist and Gordon being rowed across a lake in the spectacular scenery of Patagonia to pull off another job. Settling in at his new home, Gordon, a dandy, soon builds a secret passageway in his new home to escape from his house and spy on his own family, adopting the self-assumed airs of a quietly dashing domestic James Bond. In real life, Gordon joined Argentina’s military intelligence services as a secret agent in 1968, became a leader of pre-Junta dictatorship Triple A death squads, then, from May to November 1976, director of Automotores Orletti, one of the regime’s most heinous subversive detention and torture centers. How such a monster as Gordon, a car thief in his youth, scaled the ladder of power in 1970s’ Argentina is one of the most pertinent questions the Netflix series seeks to explain. “Gordon” is produced by Adrián Suar, a driving force in Argentine film-TV as an actor, producer at Pol-ka Producciones (“Son of the Bride,” “Violetta”) and former Canal 13 programmer. Suar produces “Gordon” with Diego Andraznik his partner at their new production house, Preludio Producciones. Trapero and De la Serna unpacked “Gordon” in the buildup to its Netflix release on Nov. 18, when it is sure to make an impact. Part of the attraction of classic crime shows is that the forces of order trap the criminal and explain their criminality. Part of the fascination of “Gordon’’ is that he becomes part of the forces of order…. Pablo Trapero : The idea of “Gordon” was to begin with fiction with real events providing their context. Gordon carries the story from beginning to end. He’s like a sci-fi portal , opening doors to Argentina’s different universes of the time. So the most difficult and highly attractive challenge was to make viewers want to watch more about a villain who becomes ever more villainous, for the audience to feel ever more emotion and commitment to the series. Rodrigo de la Serna : What’s interesting about Gordon is that he’s the only character who doesn’t have an ideology nor doctrine in a context of a Cold War between the U.S. and Soviet Republic where Peronism positions itself as a third option – neither capitalism to one extreme and Marxism to the other. Camila Peralta in ‘Gordon’ Cr. Marcos Ludevid / Netflix ©2026 MARCOS LUDEVID 2025 So what drove him? De la Serna : Gordon is a mercenary whose only interest was to be able to make money and experience the pleasure of exercising his true psychopathological essence. The national and international context allowed psychopaths of the magnitude of Gordon to reach places of power, make them their own, take off their masks and become the true monsters they are. It was much easier during these years. Trapero : What we suggest is that during these years, and not just in Argentina, the relationship with violence and the value of human life appeared to change. For Gordon and almost the period, violence became a commodity, without the gravity and consequences which violence really has. De la Serna : From 1955, when Argentina’s Navy bombed the Plaza de Maya, killing 400 people, to oust Perón from power, from this foundational act, the country’s rule of law is replaced by the rule of violence. It begins to be politically legitimate to kidnap and kill people and as Pablo says, violence becomes a commodity. People like Gordon can take off their masks and be the monster they have inside. Pablo, you wrote “Gordon” with Marcos Osorio Vidal, based on the novel by Marcelo Larraquy. How did you attempt to structure the series? Trapero : With the screenplay and in direction, we attempted to change genre from one episode to another so that viewers could follow the story via familiar cinema codes. Episode 1 is like a Western, where a stranger arrives and has to carve out his place, Episode 2 like a secret agent investigative thriller. Without giving spoilers, the last episode nears horror, with beats you can find in the genre. This renews the series’ interest, not only because of Gordon’s story but Argentina’s. To what extent could Gordon be seen as a return to the world and the mix of film noir and melodrama of “The Clan”? Trapero : I’m really a fan noir, a great genre, and melodrama, and here there’s a mix of these two so classic genres where viewers see things that are really dramatic but from a narrative point of view this makes viewing easier despite the subject. And it’s interesting you mention “The Clan.” It was a breakout which made me rethink many things. So much so that I began to make series from then on because, paradoxically, “The Clan” was a hit. I was left, however, with the sensation that I wanted to talk a lot more about this world and that the length of a film wasn’t sufficient, what was needed by the story and the characters. And Gordon offered a kind of return? Trapero : With time I understood that “Gordon” was in a way a revenge, allowing me to return to a similar period, tone and universe, with more time for us and for viewers, to contradict our own sentiments, which is what I think is happening when people watch “Gordon.” In one episode, they feel something about an issue and in another the opposite. In one episode, viewers are annoyed, in anther react in a more relaxed fashion. Rodrigo has delivered a magnificente performance in the sense of fascinating an audience – as we’re beginning to see is the case – with a story which asks so much of viewers. Rather like with “The Clan,” the paths sometimes recommended to attract audiences aren’t those of “Gordon.” Could you give an example? Trapero: If something was predictable, we tried going the other way, to see how it worked. In this sense the work of Rodrigo is extraordinary, how he gets viewers to follow Gordon. And the rest of the cast as well. Because it’s a story which depends a lot on an audience identifying with a tale which is foreign to them. There’s not one character in the series from beginning to end with whom you ca feel identified with, how they conceive the world. Perhaps a little bit with one at some time, a little bit with another at another moment, but it’s very difficult. What were the keys to your performance, Rodrigo? De la Serna : An absolute lack of empathy for others, an “anti-conscience,” you could call it. For an actor, it was an immense challenge This is the darkest role that I’ve ever had. It very close to a vampire or a demon, or he really was a demon, the darkest shadow which a people have dreamed. The Argentine people has its luminous side, but also produces this type of monster. I had to focus on Gordon’s psychopathology. He’s a compendium of all the pervasions I could cover and conceive, like a man who loses what is considered humanity: empathy with others, or an effort to work for a common good, which is what other characters are attempting. He’s a psychopath and perverse, enjoying others’ suffering. And your aims as a director, Pablo? Trapero : The large challenge from early on in the screenplay was how to cover a period which is so dark and so little visited: in audio-visual fiction, there are very few references to this period of Gordon’s life covered by the episodes. It was like opening a Pandora’s box, touching a taboo, something you couldn’t talk about out of fear and the complexes it generates. That drove our writing. Using fiction, we also wanted to bring the youngest generations something which might appear fit for history books, so that we don’t forget about what happens with violence. Sometimes in slogans or on social media violence seems abstract, but it’s beside us all the time and our duty as citizens is to care for others. ‘Gordon’ Cr. Marcos Ludevid / Netflix ©2026 MARCOS LUDEVID 2025 Nate Bargatze Returns to Netflix With New Special ‘Good for Nathan’ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...
